metric_rationale: Identifies trials where Tallying predicts a perfect tie (because both options win on exactly 1 feature) but WADD predicts a strong preference (due to differences in cue validities). The metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with WADD's favored option in these specific 'Tally-tied' trials. Tallying will yield ~0.5, while WADD will yield a value significantly greater than 0.5.

This metric isolates trials where Tallying predicts a perfect tie (i.e., both options win on an equal number of features). For these trials, Tallying must guess, producing an expected choice probability of 0.5 regardless of its parameters. In contrast, WADD uses the validities as weights to break the tie, consistently favoring the option with the higher weighted sum. By computing the proportion of choices that align with WADD's prediction on these specific trials, we expect Tallying to score around 0.5 and WADD to score significantly higher.

Measures the proportion of choices that align with Take-The-Best (TTB) on a subset of 'compensatory' trials where WADD's subjective feature weighting could lead to the opposite choice. TTB is strictly non-compensatory and lexicographic, so it will show near-100% alignment on these trials, whereas WADD will show lower alignment due to variance in subjective weights across subjects.

This metric isolates a single, highly discriminative 'compensatory' trial (Trial 11). On this trial, the single most valid feature (validity 0.95) strongly favors Option A. Take-The-Best (TTB) uses a lexicographic rule and will reliably choose Option A, resulting in a mean response near 0 (modulo lapse rate). In contrast, the Weighted Additive rule (WADD) integrates all features. The combined validity of the features favoring Option B (0.58 + 0.55 = 1.13) outweighs the single feature favoring Option A (0.95). Because WADD's random feature weights are independently drawn, the sum of the weighted evidence for B will frequently exceed the weighted evidence for A, causing WADD to choose Option B (response 1) on average more than 50% of the time. This creates a massive gap in expected choice proportion between the two models.

Since the two theories share an identical decision rule (Take-The-Best) but may differ in their parameter priors or lapse rate distributions (epsilon), measuring the overall adherence to the strict TTB prediction will effectively discriminate between them based on their implied noise levels.
Computes the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the predictions of the Take-The-Best heuristic, using the specified validity order (features 0, 2, 1, 3).

This metric calculates the difference in adherence to the Take-The-Best (TTB) prediction between trials where the Logistic Choice Model (WADD) has a large difference in weighted sums vs. a small difference. TTB predicts equal choice certainty across both sets of trials because it relies on a single discriminating cue in both cases (yielding a metric near 0). WADD predicts much lower choice certainty on the 'low difference' trials, resulting in a large positive metric.

This metric exploits the variance in choice determinism predicted by the Logistic Choice Model (WADD). We partition trials into 'Strong' (where the WADD value difference between options is large) and 'Weak' (where the WADD value difference is very small). Under TTB, all these trials are resolved decisively by a single discriminating feature, predicting equal accuracy (TTB-consistency) across both sets (difference ~ 0). WADD predicts choices will be much more deterministic on Strong trials than on Weak trials, leading to a strongly positive difference.
